title: One thing I know (John 9:13–41)
hook: whereas I was blind, now I see

segments.voice: Yesterday, Siloe, the pool called Sent: mud on the eyes and the man born blind. Your line was go, wash. Did you turn a whose-fault question into a what-now question? Day five hundred eleven.

The man has barely begun to see when the questions start. He's questioned by religious authorities, then questioned again. His parents are summoned, and they're too frightened to speak for him. By the end he has been thrown out. The healing takes two verses. The argument about it fills the rest of the chapter, and it's mostly a trial. And the man who used to beg by the road turns out to have a sharp tongue.
screen: `FIRST, HE SEES.` → `THEN, THE QUESTIONS.` → `THEN, THROWN OUT.`

segments.voice: The healing happened on a Sabbath, and the Pharisees are divided. Some say a man who doesn't keep the Sabbath can't be from God. Others ask how a sinner could do such signs. They call the man back a second time and press him: give glory to God; we know this man is a sinner. And he answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "If he be a sinner, I know not: one thing I know, that whereas I was blind, now I see." He doesn't argue theology. He doesn't claim to know everything. He knows one thing, from the inside. When they ask him to tell it all again, he asks, with a straight face, whether they want to become his disciples too. Watch how he grows through the chapter. At first, Jesus is the man that is called Jesus. Then, he is a prophet. Then, a man from God. They put him out. And Jesus, hearing of it, goes looking for him, and asks if he believes in the Son of God. Who is he, Lord, that I may believe? You have seen him, Jesus says, and it is he that talketh with thee. "And he said: I believe, Lord. And falling down, he adored him." From a name, to a prophet, to Lord. Some readers think the fear of being put out of the synagogue also reflects painful conflicts in the communities John was writing for. The Church reads the chapter as a story about sight that grows: the one who was blind sees more and more, and those sure they could see are asked whether they really do.
screen: `THE PHARISEES ARE DIVIDED.` · `ONE THING I KNOW.` · `A NAME, A PROPHET, FROM GOD, LORD.` · `I BELIEVE, LORD.` · then, large: `WHEREAS I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing you now see. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the past few months on this path, or in your life. Find one thing you see now that you didn't before. About a person. About yourself. About God, or about a story you thought you knew. Not everything. One thing. Say it plainly to yourself, the way he did: whereas I was blind, now I see this. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let it be named. The bell holds the time.
One thing I know. The healed man's answer to his questioners: I don't know everything, but whereas I was blind, now I see. Today's word.

Your line: now I see. Today, tell someone one thing you see now that you didn't. And that's week seventy-three: words of eternal life, rivers, light, truth, I am, Siloe, and one thing I know. Day five hundred eleven.
screen: `WEEK SEVENTY-THREE: ETERNAL LIFE · RIVERS · LIGHT · TRUTH · I AM · SILOE · NOW I SEE`

howItsDone: Catholics hear the whole of John 9, the trial as well as the healing, in the longer form of the Gospel on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in Year A.

fork.setup: you were blind this morning. now authorities press you: we know this man is a sinner. what do you say?
options: I don't know about that; one thing I know: I was blind, now I see.
fork.reveal: "If he be a sinner, I know not: one thing I know, that whereas I was blind, now I see." he speaks only of what he knows.

trapdoor: what you thought: a short healing story.
what it means: a long trial in which a man's sight, and his faith, grow while his questioners grow more sure they see.
what a scholar hears: the man's titles for Jesus climb from 'a man' to 'prophet' to 'Lord'; some readers hear in the expulsion the conflicts of the communities John wrote for.

notes: Week seventy-three counted as days 505–511; confirm the look-back list.
Softened in review to 'one of the longest single stories in John's Gospel' (John 4:1–42 is about as long as John 9). Confirm.
Synagogue expulsion (9:22) as possibly reflecting later community conflicts is a mainstream scholarly view; framed as 'scholars note… may'. Confirm it fits the path and Nostra Aetate.
Progression of titles (9:11 the man called Jesus; 9:17 prophet; 9:33 from God; 9:38 Lord). Confirm.
Pharisees presented as divided (9:16) to avoid a monolithic foil. Confirm.

Confirm Douay 9:35.
